title: English Vocabulary 1 · Units 52–53
description: Units 52–53 checked against the teaching pages, illustrations, exercises and answer key. Covers expressions of time and frequency, the past/present/future, spatial adverbs and prepositions, positional nouns, and distinctions between out, away and abroad. Original English examples, Brazilian Portuguese translations and British English IPA.
sourceNotice: The supplied textbook was used to check teaching and exercise targets; illustrative examples and explanations are newly written, and source exercises and images are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 52 teaching sections A–C and exercises 52.1–52.5; Unit 53 teaching sections A–E, positional illustrations and exercises 53.1–53.5. Compared exercises with the printed answer key and reviewed each original vocabulary entry, contextual translation, example, note and IPA.
audit.pronunciation: British English, primarily non-rhotic IPA, cross-checked for relevant indexed headwords in the supplied textbook phonemic index. Phrase-level IPA may have natural connected-speech and stress variants.
audit.cannotGuarantee: Local JSON and structural checks were performed. The VocabLab 1.2 Lite importer, browser text-to-speech and recording, adaptive review and backup/restore were not executed; phrase pronunciations cannot be certified by an independent dictionary in this review.

units.title: Unit 52 — Time words
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 52. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: I am studying English now.
items.note: Now refers to the present moment. Contrast then, which refers to a different time.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: I lived in Oxford then, but I live in Leeds now.
items.note: Then often refers to a time in the past; it may also mean next in a sequence. Do not confuse then and than.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: I cannot talk at this moment.
items.note: At this moment has the same present-time sense as now; it appears as an explanation on the teaching page.

items.pt: há ...; ... atrás (tempo decorrido desde um evento passado)
items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: I spoke to her ten minutes ago.
items.note: Put ago after a length of time to say how long before now something happened. It usually goes with the past simple.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: The bus left an hour ago.
items.note: Hour starts with a vowel sound because h is silent, so say an hour. Ago refers back from now.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: I finished my breakfast four hours ago.
items.note: Four hours ago means four hours before the present moment, not a period continuing until now.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: They bought the flat two years ago.
items.note: Two years ago means two years before now. This phrase is a pedagogical example of the taught ago pattern.

items.pt: por dois anos; durante dois anos
items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: I worked in a bookshop for two years.
items.note: For introduces duration, answering How long? It does not by itself identify the beginning or end.

items.pt: por três anos; durante três anos
items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: She lived in Canada for three years.
items.note: For three years expresses a duration; exercise 52.1 practises this construction.

items.pt: de; desde (ponto inicial de um intervalo)
items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: The museum is open from nine o’clock.
items.note: From introduces the starting point of a time span; it is often paired with to.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: We studied together from April to June.
items.note: To identifies the endpoint of a period in the pattern from ... to ....

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: The town had a small cinema from 2014 to 2016.
items.note: From ... to ... gives the start and end of a period. These years are usually read twenty fourteen and twenty sixteen.
items.speechText: from twenty fourteen to twenty sixteen

items.pt: passado(a); último(a), em referência a tempo
items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: We met last Friday.
items.note: Last + time period means the previous one. Do not add an article or preposition before last week/year.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: I started my new job last year.
items.note: Last year means the year before this year; it commonly occurs with past-tense verbs.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: My sister visited us last week.
items.note: Last week refers to the previous week, not the coming week.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: We went to the cinema last Saturday.
items.note: Use a capital letter for Saturday. Last Saturday refers to the previous Saturday.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: We had three tests last month.
items.note: Last month is the month before the current month; contrast next month.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: My cousin is coming next Thursday.
items.note: Next + time period refers to the following occurrence, usually in the future.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: I hope to travel next year.
items.note: Next year is the year after this one; no in or the is needed before the expression.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: We have a meeting next week.
items.note: Next week means the week after the current week.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: They are planning a holiday next summer.
items.note: Next summer refers to the coming summer; summer is normally lowercase.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: My course finishes next month.
items.note: Next month is the month after the current month; compare last month.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: Life was very different in the past.
items.note: The past is the time before now. The can be used in the past and the past, present and future.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: In the past, many people wrote letters by hand.
items.note: In the past refers to an earlier time or earlier times; it is not the same as ago + period.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: The present is a good time to learn a new skill.
items.note: The present refers to the current period. As a noun, present has first-syllable stress.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: No one knows exactly what the future will bring.
items.note: The future is the time after now; in many contexts we do not know exactly what it will bring.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: Cars may look different in the future.
items.note: In the future means at some time after now; compare in the past.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: The city grew quickly in the twentieth century.
items.note: A century is one hundred years; this word is used in the matching exercise 52.2.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: The railway opened in the nineteenth century.
items.note: The nineteenth century covers 1801–1900. The numbering of centuries is one ahead of their initial two year-digits.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: We live in the twenty-first century.
items.note: The twenty-first century covers 2001–2100. Use an ordinal number with century.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: People may use new kinds of transport in the twenty-second century.
items.note: The twenty-second century covers 2101–2200 and is the future period in the exercise.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: Many important buildings were built in the eighteenth century.
items.note: The eighteenth century covers 1701–1800 and is in the past.

items.section: A · Time in relation to now
items.example: My grandfather was born in the twentieth century.
items.note: The twentieth century covers 1901–2000; it is in the past at the time of this book.

items.example: I always brush my teeth before bed.
items.note: Always means on every relevant occasion. Frequency adverbs usually go before a main verb, but after be.

items.example: We usually eat dinner at seven.
items.note: Usually means in most cases, but not necessarily always. It generally comes before the main verb.

items.example: They often travel by train.
items.note: Often means frequently, more than sometimes but not always. The t is usually silent in the British pronunciation taught here.

items.example: I sometimes have tea with breakfast.
items.note: Sometimes means on some occasions. It is less frequent than often and more frequent than rarely.

items.example: We go to the beach now and then.
items.note: Now and then means occasionally or from time to time, not the sequence now, then.

items.example: She occasionally works on Saturdays.
items.note: Occasionally means from time to time. The frequency scale places it below sometimes.

items.example: I do not often eat in restaurants.
items.note: Not often means infrequently. The negative affects the frequency of the activity.

items.example: He rarely watches television.
items.note: Rarely means not often or seldom, but not quite never. It is a low-frequency adverb.

items.example: I never drink coffee in the evening.
items.note: Never means at no time or on no occasions. Do not normally add another negative with it.

items.example: I visited the museum once.
items.note: Once means one time. In frequency expressions, say once a week, not one time a week in the standard model.

items.example: I called my aunt twice yesterday.
items.note: Twice means two times. In frequency expressions, say twice a day rather than two times a day in the taught model.

items.example: I go swimming once a week.
items.note: Once a week means one occurrence each week. Notice a before week.

items.example: I wash my face twice a day.
items.note: Twice a day means two occurrences every day, not a duration of two days.

items.example: We visit our grandparents three times a year.
items.note: For three or more occurrences, use number + times + a + period; one and two normally use once and twice.

items.example: Our team meets four times a month.
items.note: Four times a month describes frequency, not the duration of an event.

items.example: I have piano lessons twice a week.
items.note: Twice a week means two occurrences each week; exercise 52.5 uses a two-day schedule.

items.example: Our book club meets once a month.
items.note: Once a month means one occurrence in each month; this pattern is used in exercise 52.5.

items.example: They have business meetings in Germany six times a year.
items.note: Six times a year is the frequency inferred from six listed months in exercise 52.5.

items.example: They practise tennis three times a week.
items.note: Three times a week means an activity happens on three occasions per week, as in exercise 52.5.

items.example: I practise pronunciation every morning and every evening.
items.note: Every morning and every evening gives two occasions each day, so it can be summarised as twice a day.

items.pt: daqui a pouquinho; em um instante
items.example: I will call you back in a moment.
items.note: In a moment refers to the near future: very soon. It differs from at the moment.

items.example: My brother is working at the moment.
items.note: At the moment means now or currently. It does not mean after a short wait.

items.example: I hope to see you soon.
items.note: Soon refers to a short time from now, though the length is not exact.

items.example: We moved to a new flat recently.
items.note: Recently refers to a short time before now. In British English it can appear with the past simple or present perfect.

items.pt: todos os anos; a cada ano
items.example: We spend a weekend in the countryside every year.
items.note: Every year indicates regular repetition, but does not tell us how many times within each year.

items.pt: em alguns minutos; daqui a poucos minutos
items.example: The film will start in a few minutes.
items.note: In a few minutes refers to a short time in the future; exercise 52.4 uses it to explain in a moment.

items.example: My sister is staying in Bath for two more years.
items.note: For two more years describes how much longer a situation will continue; this is practised in exercise 52.1.

learningObjectives: Refer to the present, an earlier time and the future using now, then, ago, last and next.
Distinguish ago for time before now, for for duration, and from ... to ... for a bounded period.
Place dates and centuries in the past, present or future.
Express habitual frequency using always, usually, often, sometimes, occasionally, rarely and never.
Use once, twice and number + times with a day, week, month or year.
Contrast at the moment, in a moment, soon and recently in natural speech.

units.title: Unit 53 — Places
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 53. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: Please come here and look at this photo.
items.note: Here refers to the speaker's location. Contrast there, another location.

items.example: Come here for a moment, please.
items.note: Come expresses motion towards the speaker or another relevant point; here marks the destination without to.

items.example: My sister lives in Cardiff, and I visit her there.
items.note: There refers to another place. In this unit it is a place word, not the introductory there in there is.

items.example: We can go there after lunch.
items.note: Go there is natural; do not say go to there. There is an adverb of place.

items.example: Can you take it there tomorrow?
items.note: Take something there means carry it to another place; exercise 53.1 includes this pattern.

items.pt: de volta; para o local anterior
items.example: I will be back from the shops before dinner.
items.note: Back expresses a return to a previous place or situation; the noun sense the back of is different.

items.example: Please come back before seven.
items.note: Come back means return to the speaker's place or a previous location.

items.example: I can bring it back on Monday.
items.note: Bring something back means return it to a person or place. With a pronoun, say bring it back.

items.pt: por toda parte; em todos os lugares
items.example: There were old photographs everywhere.
items.note: Everywhere means in or to all places within an area, not one specific place.

items.pt: ir ao exterior; viajar para outro país
items.example: We hope to go abroad in December.
items.note: Go abroad means travel to another country. Abroad does not need to: not go to abroad.

items.example: The children are in the kitchen.
items.note: Use in for being inside a room or area and for towns, cities, countries and continents.

items.example: My father is making soup in the kitchen.
items.note: In the kitchen means inside the room where food is prepared.

items.example: There is a small library in the village.
items.note: Use in with a village, city or other geographical area.

items.example: My cousin studies in Seoul.
items.note: Use in before a city's name; Seoul is the capital of South Korea.

items.example: Do you have a desk in your bedroom?
items.note: In your bedroom locates something inside that room; exercise 53.2 practises this use.

items.pt: em; num local ou ponto de referência
items.example: I am waiting for you at the station.
items.note: At often identifies a specific place or meeting point, instead of an enclosed area or surface.

items.example: We met at the station at noon.
items.note: At the station identifies a location; the same pattern is used in the meeting-point examples.

items.pt: na rodoviária; na estação de ônibus
items.example: I will wait for you at the bus station.
items.note: At the bus station is the location used in exercise 53.2. It is a meeting point, not a surface.

items.pt: na frente; na parte da frente (de um espaço)
items.example: The teacher is standing at the front.
items.note: At the front identifies a position at the forward part of a place or group.

items.word: at the front of the class
items.pt: na frente da sala de aula
items.example: We usually sit at the front of the class.
items.note: At the front of the class describes the front part of a classroom; contrast at the back of the class.

items.word: at the back of the class
items.pt: no fundo da sala de aula
items.example: Some students are sitting at the back of the class.
items.note: At the back of the class is the opposite of at the front of the class; exercise 53.2 practises at.

items.pt: em; sobre; apoiado em uma superfície
items.example: The newspaper is on the table.
items.note: Use on for an object touching or resting on a surface, such as a photo on a wall.

items.example: There is a small clock on the wall.
items.note: Pictures and photographs displayed against a wall are on the wall in this context.

items.example: My backpack is on the chair.
items.note: On the chair means resting on its seat or another surface; contrast in the chair in different contexts.

items.example: Please sit on the sofa.
items.note: Use on with a sofa in the seating example from exercise 53.2.

items.example: We can see the town from the top of the hill.
items.note: The top is the highest part of something. The illustrated mountain shows the top of the mountain.

items.pt: o topo de; a parte de cima de
items.example: The top of the tree is very high.
items.note: The top of is followed by a noun. Use a full phrase such as the top of the mountain in speech practice.

items.example: There is a small island in the middle of the lake.
items.note: The middle is the central part of something. The teaching illustration shows the middle of the road.

items.example: She stopped in the middle of the road.
items.note: In the middle of + noun locates something in the central part; exercise 53.5 also uses this pattern.

items.example: There is some water at the bottom of the glass.
items.note: The bottom is the lowest part. The book illustrates the bottom of a glass.

items.pt: no fundo de; na parte de baixo de
items.example: My keys were at the bottom of my bag.
items.note: At the bottom of + noun identifies a low position; this full prepositional pattern is a teaching extension.

items.example: The front of the car is damaged.
items.note: The front is the forward part; contrast the back and the side.

items.pt: a frente de; a parte dianteira de
items.example: The front of the bus has a large window.
items.note: The front of + noun identifies the forward part of an object, illustrated with a car and practised with a bus.

items.example: There is a small mark on the side of the car.
items.note: The side is the lateral part of an object; the car illustration shows it in profile.

items.pt: a lateral de; o lado de
items.example: The number is written on the side of the bus.
items.note: The side of + noun identifies the lateral part, as in the bus illustration in exercise 53.3.

items.example: The back of the car is red.
items.note: The back of + noun is the rear part, not the directional adverb back meaning return.

items.example: There are useful instructions at the beginning of the book.
items.note: Beginning means the first part. It can describe a road, a book or a time period.

items.pt: no começo de; no início de
items.example: The glossary is at the beginning of the guide.
items.note: At the beginning of + noun identifies the starting part; exercise 53.5 asks for the beginning of the book.

items.example: You can find the answers at the end of the book.
items.note: End is the final part or point. Contrast beginning, the starting part.

items.pt: no fim de; no final de
items.example: There is a café at the end of the street.
items.note: At the end of + noun identifies the final part or endpoint; exercise 53.5 practises this expression.

items.example: Please raise your left hand.
items.note: Left identifies the left-hand side; in this unit it does not mean the past form of leave.

items.example: My right hand is cold.
items.note: Right identifies the right-hand side; in other contexts right may mean correct.

items.example: He has a ring on his left hand.
items.note: Left hand is the hand on the left side of a person's body; use left before the noun.

items.example: She held the book in her right hand.
items.note: Right hand is the hand on the right side of a person's body; contrast left hand.

items.example: The bookshop is on the left.
items.note: On the left refers to a position on the left side of a road or scene, as illustrated by the cinema.

items.example: The library is on the right.
items.note: On the right refers to a position on the right side, as illustrated by the restaurant.

items.example: I want to go home now.
items.note: Home means a person's place of residence. Go home does not take to before home.

items.example: My sister is at home today.
items.note: At home means in one's house or flat. Contrast out, away and abroad.

items.example: He is out, but he will return shortly.
items.note: Out can mean temporarily not at home, for example at the shops or at work.

items.example: Mum is out at the shops.
items.note: Be out means not be at home for a short time; compare be away for a longer absence.

items.pt: ausente; fora por mais tempo; longe
items.example: They are away for a few days.
items.note: Away suggests absence for a longer time, for example on holiday; it need not mean another country.

items.pt: ir embora; sair por um período; viajar
items.example: We are going away for the weekend.
items.note: Go away can mean leave home for several days, as in exercise 53.4; it need not mean go abroad.

items.example: My brother studies abroad.
items.note: Abroad means in or to another country. Do not use in abroad or to abroad.

items.example: She wants to work abroad next year.
items.note: Work abroad means work in another country, the situation introduced in exercise 53.4.

items.example: My parents are abroad this month.
items.note: Be abroad means be in another country, unlike the wider meanings of out and away.

items.pt: sair de casa; sair para algum lugar
items.example: We sometimes go out for dinner on Friday evenings.
items.note: Go out means leave home or go somewhere for leisure. This additional sense is an extension, not a principal target of Unit 53.

learningObjectives: Distinguish here, there, back and everywhere when identifying destinations or locations.
Choose in, at and on for towns, rooms, meeting points, seating and surfaces.
Describe locations using top, middle, bottom, front, side, back, beginning and end.
Identify left-hand and right-hand positions using left, right, on the left and on the right.
Distinguish at home, out, away and abroad, including short absences, holidays and other countries.
Use come back, bring it back, go away and go abroad with natural word order and no unnecessary prepositions.
